notes.title: Weekly Update 62 - Exploration Paths
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/e5e45124e2b1bcf1008ded23ce97b028e18d2481.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
Things have been progressing steadily last week. I’ve made some changes to the shaders to make the new biomes look better, and I’ve also built quite a few new paths to explore - which is what I want to talk about today.

Essentially, the exploration side of the game has come about through the experience we’ve had with the game early on. We realised that running around on an island world from a first person perspective necessarily brought with it a desire to explore the surroundings and get an advantage from this - even when it doesn’t strictly fall into the traditional aspects of the RTS genre. Especially finding new mineral deposits and chests turned into a really fun aspect of the game, and we wanted to double down on this when creating our new island. Part of this might have been excitement about creating our own worlds and the assets which populated them - but we find it persisted beyond our expectations and carried across to our players too.

As a result, we decided to hide quite a few possible rewards and cool views across the island, to be discovered by players as they are exploring the world. This comes with a few important considerations which we are still working through:

[h3]Rewards[/h3]
Since all of our rewards are random, we quickly realised that following a long path up a mountain only to find… nothing, is quite frustrating. In general, we think that getting some form of payoff whenever the player decides to go off on a tangent from their initial path is quite important. Likewise it is important that there is at least the chance of getting a substantial reward, otherwise going off on these excursions does not make any sense. We are still working on the balance regarding what we put at the end of the paths, but we will at least attempt to take these realisations into account. We have plenty of ideas for rewards which make the effort worthwhile. We just need to balance it and maintain a level of surprise rather than an expectation.

[h3]Accessibility[/h3]
While putting rewards at the end of paths is one thing, another important consideration is how easy it is to get to these paths. We’ve all played games in which a perfectly scalable hill or small fence turns out to be an invisible wall - which can be quite frustrating, especially if a similarly looking hill right next to it can be walked up. However, if we do not constrain where players can go, a player could potentially walk up a hill we never intended to be scalable, only to be met with the frustration of finding nothing. We therefore need to carefully consider how easy we make it to follow each path, and how easy we make it to traverse a part of the map that isn’t a path at all. 

[h3]Identifiability[/h3]
Considering the above, a good compromise solution may be to make the paths more easily identifiable. If we place subtle hints along the path as to where the path is going and that the player is in fact following a path, it may make it less frustrating to explore. The player can easily tell when they are following a path that will yield a reward, and when they are just scaling a hill for a better vantage point or to cut across the map to get somewhere quicker. We haven’t quite figured out how to mark the paths, but this may be a way to get around both the issue of rewards and the issue of accessibility. We have had thoughts, like specific flowers, or particle effects - or even ground texture differences, though we are yet to commit to our approach!

As we keep building the world, I will keep adding more interesting paths to explore, and will keep you updated on what we decide regarding the points above!

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 61 - More Sounds
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/c6a66c05f8a6d8f58ce90df230ecf66fe633ef16.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
World building is progressing, but I haven’t quite finished the latest biome yet, so there isn’t a lot to show this week. As a result, I want to talk a little bit about a topic that’s been running in parallel to the remaining development: sounds!

When we initially released the game into early access (and I believe this is still mostly the case on the active branch), there were very limited sounds giving players feedback on their actions, and we only had the main menu theme in terms of music. Shooting a gun made a sound, the waves and forests gave some ambience, but largely, the game was fairly quiet. 

By now, Haakon has provided us with a whole list of sounds to use throughout the game (more animal sounds, sounds to use in the village, sounds for UI feedback, etc), and I have managed to implement about half of them on the experimental branch. I decided to initially focus on “feedback” sounds, such as the sounds when demolishing a building (see today’s image for an example ;)), selecting a blueprint, etc., which has already helped to really improve what it feels like to interact with the game. 

In the next step, I will be adding a lot more of the environmental sounds, especially throughout the village, which should make the game feel a bit more immersive (e.g. creaking of the windmill, sounds of fire, work sounds, etc.). Of course there are more places for environmental sounds (e.g. waterfalls, ponds, different types of forests), so I’m excited about adding those, too.

Finally, Haakon has also been working on composing quite a few new pieces of music to use throughout the game. We’ve been structuring them into base building music which you will be able to hear around the village, exploration music which you will be hearing across the world, and combat music to play when you are dealing with the pirates. Especially for the base building music, we are planning to also show progression through the music, so it will be starting with pieces that have only a few instruments, and will gradually build to utilising full orchestras as your village grows. 

By the time we bring 0.8 onto the experimental branch next month, you should already find some of the music in the game, but we are planning to have yet more for the February release!

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 60 - The Timeline to 0.8
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/d0524fbc922fce28386ca3ff2b1452ea9c2e5df9.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
John and I did some testing of performance and gameplay of the first two biomes of Pirate’s Peak this week, and as a result, I decided to communicate what we are currently thinking in terms of a timeline for the release of 0.8:

First of all, our work to optimise performance over Spike Ridge seems to have mostly worked out. The performance on John’s (pretty old) laptop was very encouraging, especially on lower settings, though testing on macOS showed some issues we’ll need to fix. 

Secondly, we did not run into any game-breaking bugs or issues during our playtime, which was again very encouraging considering how many large new systems I had introduced since our last major playtests. There were a few smaller issues I will need to sort out (like properly displaying rivers and streams on the tactical and strategic map), but none of that should be taking me too long. 

As a result, we don’t anticipate that any major work beyond world-building needs to be done before we can release 0.8 to you! At the moment, we are therefore expecting to release the update onto the experimental branch in December (aiming for a release before Christmas), with a full release planned for early February (after we can address any bugs, performance issues, and other problems you may find). 
If there aren’t too many issues to be found (I wish), we may even be able to add a few more units according to the soldier classes mentioned in Weekly Update 52 before the February release. 

With the February release, version 0.8 will have taken almost a year and a half to complete. When we had originally brought out the game last September, we had anticipated that we would probably be able to produce all 3 of our planned major versions (up to 0.10) in that time. However, having taken a lot of your feedback into account, we decided to both change the main mode of the game (from competitive PvP to PvE), and considerably upgrade our worldbuilding and progression as a result. Since 0.9 and 0.10 won’t require us to make similarly sweeping changes again, we are pretty confident that they will be done in a much shorter timespan, and we are very much looking forward to working on them soon!

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 59 - The Woodland Biome
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/86cf1ff95488c52a20cfbecdc06380f050c88309.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
I will try to keep today’s update short, and will just give you a quick overview of the second biome, the woodland valley. 

The woodland valley is the main area of player 2 (assuming you are playing coop - it is just as accessible as the grasslands for players who choose single player). Unlike the grasslands, it does not have a lot of space for expansion, and any area that you want to expand into needs to first be cleared of trees. The narrow nature of the valley also means that you are unlikely to be able to place fields here, which means that your ally from the grasslands will have to supply you with food.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/9b39aa71b392683e0922e371f88e30c06208119f.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/4433ca59bc21a8e4c4c4654b33eb2830bc5753dd.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/fed8080b5f7b3980dad891a194692e275c19274f.png[/img]

To make up for that, the biome is much richer in resources and treasure. While the grasslands may look lush, the bushes and palm trees from it do not provide a lot of wood so players trying to gather it from there will run out fairly quickly. Additionally, there are many more paths into the mountain from the valley, giving many options for exploration and to find interesting rewards! As a result, player 2 should be in a great position to send wood to their ally in return for food.

Finally, the woodland valley is also the biome that connects to the next area, the stone valleys, which players need to expand into in order to reach the more advanced stone building tier.

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 58 - The Grassland Biome
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/cc34d8b749dbd00fd23fdb2afda3873c0f25e249.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
As promised, today’s main image shows the new grasslands biome. I’ll use today’s post to show you some further views of it, explain some of our ideas, and give you another explanation of a (future) optimisation technique.

Starting off with the biome, we are intending this grassland biome to be the main source for food and farming on this map. Player 1 will start off closest to it, and it provides ample space to expand into, build fields in it, and will start off with a generous chance for banana tree groups to spawn. Below are some screenshots showing the flat space for buildings and fields:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/9b320fa414b6de7e43989b5dd1c11fc6bb0c204b.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/43f3a9122a769ad5e2f00275e91a7606c6ba0795.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/6889f4ce903cbfd4bf589505d88355f39f931375.png[/img]
Of course, there are a few hidden areas and treasures to be found in the grasslands, and while I won’t quite give their locations away, I’ll also show some of the water I placed around the biome to make looking for them a bit more enjoyable:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/838cf63238967cb1119776199001e155c8ec0320.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/651ae66bca75e72c61be8bf52293084655d40397.png[/img]
In the last picture, as well as the main one of the post, you can also see the humidity map I spoke about 2 weeks ago in action: the rocks closer to the water are more weathered and mossy, while the areas up on the mountain are a lot drier - something that will be even more apparent between biomes.

Finally, I want to also show one of the ways the biome is set up for future optimisation (when the game is a little further along and I have the time to prioritise): In a similar way to the ground cover I spoke about last week, the plants you see on the mountains, which can’t be reached by villagers, are set up that they can’t be interacted with. This allows us to cut down on overhead already, and in the future, means that we can unload them together with the mountain rocks themselves, as players are further away from them. As a result, we should then see improvements in RAM use as they get unloaded, helping us to get better performance once the full island starts to become a bit memory heavy. One example of this can be seen below:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/f09a773a96c84d8c32da3a8c8e0eb3029feeac94.png[/img]
(this is the main screenshot with an example of the middle mountain switched off for reduced memory usage)

I’ll introduce the next biome - the woodland valley - next week and will let you know some more about our other progress as well then!

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 57 - Optimising Assets
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/6d9367417c646d6c710c26fa4b3fa871fdbf799c.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
I was hoping to have a nice screenshot of the new area(s) ready for today’s update, but we still have to make some changes to the plants before we can finalise their placement, so that will have to wait until next week. Instead, I will tell you what changes we have made to the assets this week.

First of all, we are of course trying to create a beautiful island for you to walk around on. For a tropical island with jungles, grasslands, dry-ish desert areas, etc, this means many, many thousands of rocks, plants, and other objects. For Spike Ridge, we ended up having placed some 120,000 plants by the time we finished - and while that still seemed like too few objects and plants in the world, it certainly started showing in performance. Spike Ridge takes quite some time to load, and if a computer has too little memory, it ends up running rather sluggish. For our new island, we are placing even more rocks and foliage to improve the first person view experience, but that also made me somewhat worried about performance.

Of course there are many, many ways to optimise performance, and while optimisation is not yet our first priority, many of those ideas are at the back of our heads as we build systems and assets. 
For example, we had already started clustering various plants together into groups, so instead of placing thousands of individual ferns (each with its own way to handle being cut down by the player or villager), we now have groups of 5-15 ferns which are destroyed as one, massively cutting down on overhead. We decided that this was acceptable to us because frankly, on an island with 120,000 plants, pirates, and a whole town to build, we did not expect that players would be particularly bothered about whether they could cut down one individual fern vs a group of 10 (Today's image shows some individual plants on the left, grouped into one cluster on the right).

This week, we took this approach even further, and created a more generic group of “ground cover”. This ground cover will not give wood, and will be low enough not to block vision. As a result, we don’t think there is any particular reason to cut them down, and we can create them without a lot of the usual features that would interact with players and villagers, making them much more performant. Of course, the ground cover will still be removed by buildings when they are placed on top - which was one of the systems I needed to come up with this week.

More on the optimisation part (and the screenshot of the new biome) next week.

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 56 - Sweeping Animations
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/3955746dca9cff11e60d73a2312bf28c3ec6500f.jpg[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
John here again, as a diversion from the world building and rock creation which has been dominating our time of late; I made a broom and did some sweeping today. Well, the sweeping is more of an animation for our villagers and the broom creation was digital but they will be able to clean up a lot more efficiently than I will. 

There are a lot more of them after all. 

We have talked about this previously and building animations are on our roadmap. Not for 0.8 mind, but it is not only Phil that has problems overreaching and deviating from the order of his todo list. This sweeping animation will serve as the default for all of the workers for the different buildings we have. Eventually each building will have its own animations, showing that they are in use and how many people are working there. For now however, we feel it would bring more life to the village to have them utilising this idle animation so the players can better see when their buildings are processing.

We are really looking forward to how busy the villages will feel. We already have a strong sense, as players, when the village turns from a few houses at the start into a bustling home full of villagers as we are growing it. Likewise, watching our villagers marching across the island delivering goods and collecting resources really makes us feel like proud fathers, seeing our progeny busy in their daily lives. By now, we have already added a few “inanimate” animations to buildings, like smoke rising from the smelters or the windmill turning its blades - something that really adds to the feeling of a lively village as well. Being surrounded by the rest of the buildings looking equally vibrant will really develop that sense and reinforce the desire to grow our bases. We shall continue assessing how to enhance that further and let us know if you have any suggestions!

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 55 - Humidity Map
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/d19bb12d8ecfd8ae13669a855f097bf03f00c6b2.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
Last week was spent on more world building, but as part of that, I also ended up creating a new system for how the terrain rocks are coloured, which I want to talk about today.

Two weeks ago, I mentioned that our plans for 0.9 included creating a system of fertility for the islands, which will affect where fields can be placed (and where they can’t), how productive they will be, and maybe we will even introduce different fertility requirements for different crops, meaning that some areas will be great to farm coffee but can’t grow wheat, or vice versa. Two weeks ago I also mentioned that I am not always great at keeping to the order in which I’ve decided to work on things, and so I ended up doing a substantial part of the work required for this fertility system last week. 

The reason for that is relatively straightforward: We wanted different biomes to reflect different levels of humidity/aridness to allow us to have a wet, jungle environment, or a drier pine environment. The rocks we have shown you in previous posts were all set up to look rather dry and desert-like. While that look is pretty nice by itself, it doesn't necessarily fit the lush jungle feeling that we wanted from a lot of the island, nor a lot of the tropical feeling we already have in a lot of places. As a result, we wanted the colour of the rocks to change depending on the area on the island and how wet we expect this area to be - which required giving our shaders some variables for moss growth, weathering of the rock, etc.

Originally, we thought that we would simply manually set the colour of the rocks to reflect the humidity we wanted, but we realised that the strong contrast between the dryness of the rocks did not look great. Likewise, we wanted to be able to introduce at least some variety within the same biome (e.g. wetter rocks closer to streams and rivers), and we needed a different approach to making that happen than simply setting colours manually. 

This brought us to creating a humidity map. You can imagine this as a simple top down image of the island, telling the rocks where areas are wet and where areas are dry - with them adjusting their colours automatically. The result works quite well, and we will try to base further developments, such as moss on tree bark or weathering of buildings based on this map as well. 

In world building news, I have finished the mountains for the first biome, and with the humidity map done, I can start populating it with some trees and plants as well. I will also continue placing rocks for the second biome that I am almost finished with, so hopefully I should be able to get both done by next week.

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 54 - World Building
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/14dab346098ad1a6f312f898c6d13b7774936f26.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
Last week was mostly spent on world building and animations, so I want to talk to you a little bit more about what goes into our new world building. I will start by talking about the considerations that go into world building generically today, and maybe I will take another post in the coming weeks to show some specific aspects of what I’m doing with the new island.

When we designed our first island, Spike Ridge, we designed it to be viable as a competitive map for up to four players. Each player started in a different corner of the island, and particularly valuable resources could be found in the middle. However, this also meant that all players needed equal access to resources, and we had to distribute all resources across each quarter of the map, which meant that we had major constraints in designing what we wanted the world to look like. Thanks to our new coop and PvE focus, however, we do not have these constraints for the new map. The map is approximately 3 km long and 1 km wide, with both players starting next to each other on the short end, giving us plenty of room to design for progression and strategy.

As I have talked about before (and is prominently displayed on our roadmap), we like to think of the game in 3 pillars: A “survival/adventure” pillar, focused mostly around the FPS experience of the commander and exploration, a “village building” pillar, focused around placing buildings, creating supply chains, etc., and a “strategy” pillar, focused on military and competition. When designing the world, we obviously need to take all three into account and figure out how to best support each pillar with the way the world works.

Considering I have previously mentioned this as well, let’s start with the considerations of the village building pillar, which are closely linked to progression through the game: since your access to resources is largely responsible for what you can build and sell, we have decided to distribute the various mining resources across the world. Each needed resource will be found in a distinct biome, which players need to expand into in order to secure their access to it. Thanks to the new island form, advanced building materials should be found further across the island. Biomes will also be separated by mountains and rivers that will be impassable to armies and villagers (though an enthusiastic commander may manage to bunny-hop over one), making expansion more difficult to plan for.

Building on the mountains and rivers, we are also designing for strategic considerations. Early on, it will be possible to get from one biome to the other along multiple paths (mountain passes and river fords), meaning players have to secure a number of possible approaches the pirates could take. Likewise, securing any one of them should be easy, making expansion a little more pleasant to start with. As you progress through the island, biomes will be less connected, allowing you to secure your advance against the increasingly powerful pirate armies, but also forcing you to figure out how to advance when faced with their attacks along a narrow pathway.

Finally, we have to constantly consider the experience of the player in first-person view. Where a traditional RTS game doesn’t really need to build much detail into their worlds, we have much more of a need to make it interesting for our commanders to be engaged with the world. Our solution has been to create many small paths, leading up or down the mountains and cliffs and which are impassable to the villagers. At the end of each path, the player may find a reward (food, coin, seeds etc), which will make exploration interesting. As we add a tech tree to the next update (0.9), we are also planning on having some random techs as possible rewards, making exploration more important for the fate of your people (all rewards are random per game, of course).

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/46760ccdd8b0b89856afe31706fccc179604599f.png[/img]
(One of the hidden paths leading to a chest on a cliffside)

In more practical terms, we have been testing the new map and coop for quite some time. During our play, we have come to various conclusions about where we think things should be placed, where passes and barriers should be placed, and how we would like the progression to work. As a result, we have already adapted the terrain accordingly, put down mountains, decided on the layout of the rivers, and laid out the biome borders. As our next step, we have to populate the sheer mountain sides with the new rocks mentioned in previous posts. This work takes a relatively long time, but I have almost finished the mountains of the first 2 (of 6) biomes. Once this is done, we can add plants and unique elements to the biomes, finalise the paths for the commander, and add the hundreds of positions in which unique elements may spawn (chests, ore veins, pirates, etc).

As I finish some of the biomes in the coming weeks, I will provide some pictures to show what we have come up with.

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 53 - Taking Stock
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/474c438e41880d27abff3865f40bcfb9d62af34f.png[/img][h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
We noticed earlier this week that the game has now officially been out for 1 year! Time has flown past us, working on the game and everything else in our lives, but we want to use this post to take stock of the last year, as well as where we still want to go with the game.

[h3]First of all: What happened this year?[/h3]
After the game came out last year, we were able to get a lot more feedback from players than we had ever received before. We were able to fix many, many bugs, reassess some of our ideas about what the game should be, and we were able to considerably narrow down our vision for what we wanted the game to be when it was finished.

Notably, in the first half of the year, we added pirate attacks to the game, enabled multiplayer, building destruction, etc. - and decided to fully embrace the game as a PvE experience. In the second half of the year, we decided to stop regularly updating the game to focus on creating the first major update (0.8), since the many changes we were making would have repeatedly broken the live game, and many of the new features were only viable to be released together. 0.8 will be largely focused on adding more military gameplay options, making the game against the pirates more interesting (rather than just having a few waves come at you), making progression through the game more meaningful, and improving a lot of the visuals of the world. 

Finally, we managed to consistently work on the game for the entire year, despite personal and professional setbacks and responsibilities, many of which were unforeseen, and we remain incredibly enthusiastic about working on, and continuing to improve the game as much as we can!

[h3]With that, let’s move on to a brief overview of what we are currently planning: [/h3]
The obvious next step is to finalise and release 0.8. At this point, there are no new features left to add for this update. The only coding that still needs to be done is bug fixing and implementing the new animations (and sounds), which should hopefully not have too many unexpected difficulties creeping up. We also need to finalise world building our new island (and first coop-focused map), which may still take a bit of time, since meaningfully populating a 3 square kilometre world is no small task - but I will report on progress every week. 

John needs to finish up the animations. He is about 85% through creating them for 0.8 (the bulk of the work), and planning to refine them as we progress through updates. Then he needs to create 9 new building models together with their requisite icons and villager icons and get them into the game. Finally, we need to update the tutorial to explain all the new mechanics - so basically bragging about all the work we have done over the last 6 months (but in a helpful way that shows newcomers what it is all about ;) ).

Once 0.8 is released, we will focus once more on fixing bugs and responding to player feedback for a little while, (John will steadily release additional artwork in that time like additional clothing sets for different professions etc.) before moving on to the next 2 major updates:

0.9 will be an industry update, largely focusing on the base building, new fields and a fertility system (plant - not villager), production chains, and a research system (the coding for most of this is already done but not implemented yet).

0.10 will be an adventure update, focusing on the first person gameplay, adding quests, more variety in the world, Points of Interest, and maybe some procedural worldbuilding (as mentioned in previous posts, I also finished the quest system for this some time ago - I really am not very good at doing things in order).

Thank you for sticking with us and the game for this past year, and as always, we are looking forward to your feedback and will keep you updated along the next year (or so) of this journey!

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 52 - Unit Classes
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/a2bf8d488f20155c1b903626b9f1fcd05bd9ccaf.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
Work on 0.8 is progressing nicely, and I am finding more and more obscure bugs. Regardless, I want to make today’s post about some of our considerations for how to adjust our soldiers post 0.8.

As you may know from following these posts, we decided to introduce two new soldiers for 0.8, specifically the pistoleer and the swordsman. We wanted to introduce these units in addition to the existing musketeer, in order to allow more progression in the game, as well as vary the tactics players could use on the battlefield. 

And that description itself already shows where one of our problems are: The new units are now meant to address both progression through the game, and give options for varied tactics. Of course, these goals are in slight contrast with each other. If we want one unit to be an improvement over another, we would want the “upgrade” to generally beat the first unit, otherwise the progress will feel empty. At the same time, we want there to be a meaningful choice between units - so you should want to choose your units based on your current need, not only on your current level of development.

As I had alluded to in previous posts, we wanted this meaningful difference between units to come in the form of superior performance in certain biomes - the short range swordsman should win in a fight in a dense jungle, where seeing (and aiming for) an opponent is not possible until they get within melee range. Likewise, in an open plain, a charging swordsman should not be able to win against a musketeer, who has the time and sight to fire at the advancing swordsman. This has actually worked fairly well in our tests so far - positioning your swordsmen to guard a bottleneck from slightly behind the bend allows them to charge straight at their enemies as soon as they are visible - which has resulted in them defeating the generally more dangerous musketeers. 

Ideally, we would want to maintain this level of tactical decision making, without interfering with the feeling of progress at the same time. As a result, we are now thinking of adding some more units just after releasing 0.8, and generally organising them into two types of unit: the close range - and the long range units. Starting with swordsmen for close range, these could be upgraded into pistoleers (giving pistols slightly less range), and finally soldiers wielding blunderbusses (which will go nicely with the pirate theme, too). Likewise, the long range units can progress through the tiers, while maintaining their unique advantages and disadvantages compared to the short range units. 

Considering that planning out these new units, their animations, barracks, etc, will all take time, we have made the decision not to make this change until after the release of 0.8. However, once made, it will be a cleaner structure to build on, and in time, we may be able to also introduce a 3rd or 4th type of units. 

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 51 - Updating the Textures
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/2de9c3329ef58165ff3a6578bfd95cac0067de23.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
John here, I am going to take the opportunity to dive a little into some of the art processes this week. As you can see from the header image, The ammunition maker has been created for the game. A key part of the model for this artisan was the ability to reuse the texture I created for the charcoal maker which I want to speak about during this blog. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/e3d3e8209e5c063bc3719f33ce07d5806b4b1b15.png[/img]

This is the texture I created to start with. You are looking at a high resolution model with the cobblestone carved in Blender where I spent some time sculpting a tileable wall, then I used the sculpt to generate normal maps and ambient occlusion maps for the texture to be useful in Unity.

This is a useful process I’d like to talk through for those of you that are interested. And it will highlight some of my future tasks for improvement of the art within the game.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/6655f4d964e55ecb7807d2ed64a69955df862c6e.png[/img]

So I baked out this normal map from the sculpt. The different hues tell the game engine how to render the texture, to show shadow when in the light. The ambient occlusion provides information for the engine for when this texture is in shadow. Combine that information with the flat colour of the albedo map and the texture can produce a good looking wall on just a flat plane. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/5867967597028336212b20cdb875d268a1652e0b.png[/img]

The beauty here, as seen with this screenshot - is that we can change just the albedo for the texture, and it makes it appear as though we have painted over the cobblestone wall for this building, which helps to merge the different building types together. We can equally introduce other albedos for differences and variety which will be coming in a future industry update where all of our buildings will have random elements that change each time you place a building of that type. So, for instance, you could have a row of the same houses which have individual colours for the walls or different balconies, chimneys or windows in different places etc which will all help to make the village feel more organically grown and lived in. 

I have it on my to-do list to create a texture like this cobblestone for the render for the buildings (at the moment, it was rapidly done and lacks the same depth and charm) the timber roof tiles, the terracotta roof tiles and the bricks. By the time that I have finished with them, we should have a nice collection of materials which transform base models and upgrade all of our models equally. I look forward to showing you the improvements as we create them.

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 50 - Implementing the Scouts
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/47ccf3d85218ad180b4fea85172c9c88fbb5a99e.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
Last week was largely concerned with implementing the scouts, and making some adjustments to unit behaviour to align with the scouts as well.

Firstly, we implemented the scouts as described last week: they can be hired at their own barracks-type building, which comes with a version of the strategic map, and they can then be manually sent to scout areas of the map. Scouting itself happens once they arrive at their destination, and happens at a speed of 1 tile per second (1 tile is a 10x10 metre/yard area). Considering the size of the map, we chose to set scouts to reveal an area with a 200 metre radius (see today's picture), which ends up taking quite a bit of time! For now, we think this is a pretty good pace, but we may want to adjust it in the future, or allow hiring of multiple scouts from the same building to speed scouting up, so stay tuned!

Secondly, we also made some adjustments to unit behaviour to make the scouts work better: previously, units were able to detect other units at a range of up to 100 metres. This was a little problematic for 2 main reasons - A) musketeers were able to shoot at a range of 100 metres, so there was no buffer between their range to detect and their range to shoot an opponent, and B) a range of 101 metres was just a bit too short for pirates to not hear gunshots anymore.

At this point, detection range of sound has been increased to 250 metres, and line sight has been set to 150 metres (mostly for performance reasons, but it shouldn't be affecting behaviour). Together, this should lead to unit behaviour that is a little more natural than before, and help scouts detect things better.

Finally, we also adjusted stealth (yet again), to be more viable for scouts. As a result, scouts will now be able to “hide” in the closest overgrown area in order to avoid being seen (and shot) by pirates and hostile soldiers.

Following all of these changes, there now isn’t much left to go for 0.8. On my end, I primarily need to focus on polishing some features and implementations (e.g. adding the sounds Haakon created), and lots and lots of worldbuilding and bug fixing. John still has some fighting to do with the villager modelling and animation, but we are getting closer every day!

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 49 - Designing the Scouts
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/9a20fd243e06d74a11a3b82543ac690e20fc4737.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
Back on schedule with this update! Last week was largely dedicated to finding some illusive bugs, world building, and finally, to going through some design iterations for the scouts, which I want to talk about today.

When thinking about a new design, we usually try to fit the new design as closely into the existing framework as possible to make the gameplay simpler and more intuitive for players - which was a bit of a challenge for the scouts:

First of all, we needed to make a decision about what type of unit we wanted the scout to be: did we want the scout to be a type of civilian unit, to spawn in a house, and to be employed in the scouting building? Or did we want the scout to be a military unit, which spawns into the scouting building directly? Importantly here, the scout would provide military intelligence, but wouldn't fight - meaning the role doesn’t fit neatly in either category.

Secondly, we needed to decide how we wanted the scouts to behave. Did we want to have them scout the map automatically, seeking out areas that had not been revealed yet (or hadn’t been updated in a while), and to automatically update the player’s knowledge on them? Or did we want them to be manually controlled, to be sent out via the map to recon specific areas? The former makes them both easier to use, and more of a liability, considering they could repeatedly run into an enemy encampment. Likewise, the manual control would give players more choices, but potentially become tedious by the mid-game.

Ultimately, we decided that the scout will be a type of military unit, with direct, manual control by the player, similar to other soldiers. Considering the scouts will both reveal the map and serve as a means to detect enemy troop movements, we decided that we wanted to implement them as being manually controlled - that way, a player can place them in an elevated position or at a choke-point to get advance warning of enemies, even in the late game when all of the map is already revealed. 

Once we had made this decision, the direct control of the scouts, in line with soldiers, not civilian control, made us want to turn them into military units for a consistent experience. Of course, we may add a way to have them automatically explore later, but for now we hope that this approach will give the most tactical and strategic options for scout use.

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 48 - Implementing Features
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/28634471801d797c3c2289fe4084609a82da379c.jpg[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
This week’s update is a little late - I was travelling this weekend and then feeling a little under the weather. Regardless, we were able to make some decent progress implementing the new features, so I want to talk about that today.

Whenever we create new features, there are usually a few steps: First of all, we design the feature, trying to figure out what the game needs. Secondly, we try to create the new system, see how it works out, and adjust the design in whatever ways we think fits best in practice. Thirdly, I usually rewrite the “experimental” initial approach of the feature, so it is cleaner and more scalable. After this third step, I usually put it into a single building or into our experimental map (depending on the feature), and call it more or less done. However, that is a little optimistic. There is, of course, a fourth step needed, which is to also implement across the rest of the game. 

As a result, we’ve had a lot of features which hadn’t gone through the fourth step yet - something that isn’t too difficult to do, but that still requires some work to be dedicated to it before we can release the v.0.8!

Among the features I took through the fourth step this week were, for example, the strategic and tactical map. So far, the setup had only existed for our experimental coop map, but it is now available in all maps. Another implementation improvement was our multiplayer save loading. After adapting it to be local as I mentioned last week, I now also implemented that only the host can try loading it, and that every player is automatically assigned the faction that they played with before.

Another improvement was made for the mineral veins. So far, the 3 types of vein had been hard coded (iron, gold, gems). In the past week, I was able to refactor this to be able to handle any number of minerals (this will be important for the industry update (0.9) as well). Consequently, we’ve also added stone and coal as possible mineable resources already. This is something we strongly feel is needed for 0.8 already, as it will also add needed progression and a sense of satisfaction as you advance up the island.

Completing these steps gets us closer and closer to actually finishing 0.8, and we are excited about getting them ready for release!

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 47 - Charcoal, Waypoints, and Saving
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/5543e3679b0583f62f823e5a226b394e5bb9b9ef.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
Things have been fairly busy with many small things on our end, so I will just give you a quick overview of last week’s developments:

First of all, John made a new model for the Charcoal Hut (so far, we had been using a model I quickly put together myself). You can see the result in today’s picture. The Charcoal Hut is part of the new Ammo making mechanics, but we are also thinking of integrating Coal as a possible fuel source for Smelters and similar buildings.

Secondly, I was able to implement multi-waypoints for soldiers. This now means that you can give your soldiers instructions on how to get to their destination on the strategy map, set up flanking in the tactical map, or simply use a bit more finesse for your order in the standard view.

Another bigger development was a change in saving and loading for multiplayer games. Previously, our saves were small enough that the host could simply request the local data from other players when saving, which would create one single save file on the host’s computer. When loading, this save file was then sent to all of the players in the lobby, and each player could load the data for the faction they were assigned to.

Considering all of the developments of the past few months (especially the maps), the file size of our save games has increased quite a lot, and our networking solution doesn’t allow the sending of files as big as we require now. As a result, the host now requests that each player saves their data locally, which can be loaded locally when starting the game. As a result, saving and loading is much more efficient, but it won’t be possible to swap a player out halfway through the game - which we are sure is something that happens almost never anyway.

Finally, our tests of the various new mechanics have led to many bugfixes, as well as a slight rebalancing in the Ammo mechanics, and a yet more emphasised progression than what I had talked about last week.

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 46 - Progression
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/507e1bda1f8f26304e400dac89a1c4939f10a8ca.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
As over the past few weeks, we’ve made pretty good progress toward 0.8, and I want to specifically talk about biomes, progression, and to some extent the new Watchposts today.

Many of you know from these posts or from playing the game early on, that we initially designed the game to be PvP focused. With that in mind, we wanted to limit the amount of raw resources to build with, make them accessible fairly early in the game (so much so that you would often be able to access all 3 building materials from your initial base), and we even allowed purchasing them if you didn’t find enough/close-by deposits.

With our shift to PvE, we have decided to somewhat change this system, and enable players to progress in a more step-by-step nature, as they go through the game and deeper into the island(s). Specifically, we have recently decided to tie needed resources to specific areas of the island, and to move stone and metal further toward the back. As a result, players will now need to build far more of the wood-tier buildings before they can advance to stone, and finally to metal. 

This also nicely ties in with the new split of soldiers into three units: The wood tier allows players to create Swordsmen Barracks, as well as the new Swordsman Watchpost (a much cheaper alternative, which provides a Swordsman for stationary defence). Once players have built up enough money and military to advance, they can use their Swordsmen to secure and establish an outpost to get stone - which will allow them access to Pistoleers, Pistoleer Watchposts, Ammo Makers, better food production, etc. Their pistoleers will then allow them to secure an outpost in the metal rich area to access Musketeers, which will ultimately help them to secure the Artefact from the Pirates!

Of course, once we introduce additional resources and research, we can potentially create more branching advancements - Making players choose between creating an outpost that would allow them to get more food, or an outpost to get better soldiers next. 

Let us know what you think.

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 45 - Accurate Musketmen
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/c055bd781de17ed786e1dab23c2bf8ea074fd9fa.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
There have been many big changes and improvements over the past week, including implementing swordsmen and pistoleers, as well as the ammo supply mechanics, all of which I spoke about a few weeks ago. So considering I had already addressed those, I want to instead talk about a smallish change we decided on that will have much bigger consequences: Accurate shooting for soldiers.

Previously, soldiers shot in a random direction within a small cone of fire. This meant that shots were somewhat inaccurate, and the longer the range at which they were shooting, the less accurate they would be. We implemented it this way for a number of reasons, the main one being that we wanted the game to feel somewhat realistic, while at the same time not feeling unfair:

Between seeing bullets soar over your head and bullets killing with a single shot, we felt that we could get more interesting and tense battles going. This was of course aimed at battles between the player and pirates, as well as different sides, while not frustrating the player by being killed by a single, accurate bullet shot by a pirate they hadn’t even seen yet.

However, this consideration has become less relevant since. We already implemented health in the game, as well as different damage done by different units. With the new units, the high damage, long range musketman is also not going to be a unit that the player will encounter in the early game anymore - making the decision to seek them out in more dangerous biomes a conscious choice, and hopefully less frustrating.

With that said, the decision to maintain inaccurate fire became less relevant, and just left us a little frustrated. A lot of the fight ended up coming down to chance, and sometimes a single pirate would take out 3 towers, while other times, a single tower would hold off 5 pirates. This level of randomness is obviously not something that lends itself to very tactical combat, and as such, we decided to get rid of it, and leave the randomness to what pirates actually spawn and where!

Overall, this change should also help with balancing the new units, as we will now be able to tell exactly how groups of different units should perform against each other, influenced only by biomes and height - both of which are variables the player can control.

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 44 - Building Fires
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/2e06eb2787a36b20a215a63b441fab03829729c1.png[/img][h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
As the new features for 0.8 are coming along nicely, we have not only been fixing bugs, but we have also managed to do a little bit of polish - so today I will be talking about the polish for the building destruction.

Building destruction has been in the game for a little bit (it is even on the live branch), but considering that we added it very quickly, it was still missing a lot: For one, the attacks by the soldiers are lacking an animation (so they are attacking the buildings by staring at them menacingly), and there was also no feedback for the player about the state a building was in - it went from being completely fine, to being gone.

Of course we have been thinking about and working on giving more feedback to players across the board, including new UI sounds and particle effects, so the building destruction is no exception. In general, we are trying to avoid using UI elements wherever possible, and we are trying to use actual in game feedback instead. In this case, we remembered the way Age of Empires showed building damage: With fires showing on the building, which would get larger as more damage was done. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/15474493dc597f1612c5079fd67bbe6b198989ac.png[/img]
(The fire just starting)

On our end, we will be adding additional flames as building damage progresses. Initially, only a single fire will be visible, until eventually, the whole building is up in flames (compare the screenshots above). Once the building health drops below 0, the building will audibly break, and a big cloud of dust particles will show the destruction as well. For now, we are not planning on having the flames themselves do damage to the structure, so this will be purely cosmetic, with the flames disappearing one after another as villagers repair the building.

Overall, having this feedback should help make the destruction of buildings a little less sudden, and the plume of smoke being visible from afar should certainly help warn players of attacks happening even when they are out exploring the world. - We are noticing this significantly with the smoke from the pirate camp fires letting us know there is danger over the next hill and it really adds to the feel of exploring.

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 43 - Fresh Water
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/e8a0258fd2a042a732ade47e017ec0476e5244b1.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
Last week has revolved around quite a bit of bug fixing again, but we also managed to add fresh water (ponds, lakes, streams and waterfalls), and added a little to the world building.

With regards to world building, we also decided to make the world a little less random than it was before: where in the current map, you can find grassland, forests, and beaches across most of the island, the newer island will have more distinct biomes in specific locations. Each biome will also come with unique resources (for example, the grasslands will have the most access to farming, the arid mountains will have access to stone, etc), which will make expansion more needed and relevant.

While we are currently focusing the biome around the few needed resources we have (food, wood, stone, metal, and coal (which is a new resource for 0.8)), having more distinct biomes also allows us to distribute upcoming resources among them, and give a visual distinction to each area, based on the resources you may find there.

In addition, the new world building has also allowed us to create little hidden paths and areas which are inaccessible to your villagers, but in which players can find treasure if they choose to go looking for it. This should improve the feeling around exploration quite a bit, and we are looking forward to building and sharing more areas with you over the next weeks!

As always, let us know what you think.

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 42 - The Finished Strategic Map
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/3e48c629fb9a1c26cd89fd750c9783f0d8914ba9.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
We have made a lot of progress this past week, especially on fixing various bugs, but I want to bring this back to talking about maps once more, as I just finished (finally!) the map mechanics (colours and icons still subject to change ;) ).

When I last talked about the maps (in weekly update 37), I mentioned that you would not be able to see the map until you build the Military HQ. However, John and I decided to change this system slightly, since the Military HQ should be more of a late game building that enables you to command your military more efficiently.

As a result, we have decided to move the map into the Port to start with. This means that you will start off with a map (unrevealed, of course), where you will be able to check your progress in discovering the island, check where that chest or ore vein you saw 20 minutes ago was, etc. Once you have the means to create a cartographer’s hut (final name pending), you will be able to send your scouts out to help you complete the map, and will be able to see their progress whenever you check the Port.

Finally, the Military HQ will provide you with a second map (showing the same discoveries), as well as the ability to select your military units from the map, and send them to locations anywhere on the map as well. This will mean that, as you have more Barracks and soldiers toward the end of the game, you will be able to take more of a macro-perspective on ongoing battles, sending your units in the areas where they are most needed in the moment, rather than commanding them with more precision at the front lines (though that is of course still possible). 

Let me give you some examples of how this may work: for one, you could be setting up the larger scale deployments of troops from your Military HQ and getting your logistics and support in place for a campaign, after which you move to the front lines to take advantage of the set-up and to overcome a particular challenge. Alternatively, you could be taking advantage of the upcoming specialisations, focusing on the home base to organise a steady (and hopefully increasing) supply of ammo and food to your ally who is commanding at the front lines, where they could be asking you to deploy troops onto the hills or ledges where they will be most effective - We will be fascinated to see how this develops and how our players choose to use the strategic maps, but of course we will need to strike the right balance to make sure just sending troops in from the HQ will lead to a less effective (and potentially disastrous) outcome than seeing the specifics of the fight on the ground.

We hope that with this change, we give players a more rewarding early exploration experience, while maintaining a very distinct benefit and progression to building the Military HQ later. Of course, our testing in the coming weeks may lead to some additional tweaks, but we think this is a good way of handling exploration and its benefits across the length of the game. As always, let us know what you think!

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 41 - Swordsmen and Pistoleers
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/8abbefa2f429cf97858242a7accd0adfdba90b41.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
Today, I want to talk about the new units we will be introducing with version 0.8.

I mentioned a few weeks ago that we wanted to introduce Ammo as a new mechanic in order to create supply lines and to make the game more strategic overall. As I offhandedly mentioned at the time, once your soldiers run out of ammo, it will be necessary for them to engage further opponents in melee, rather than simply twiddling their thumbs while they get shot at by their opponents. However, this also means that we will be introducing melee combat for the current musketmen (using a bayonet), and we will be introducing additional units to add more options to the military part of the game and help your progression through the map as you increase the capabilities of your soldiers.

For one, we will be introducing a new melee unit, the swordsman. The swordsman will obviously not be using any ammo, and won't have a gun. He will be charging opponents to get into melee range, and will be the most effective melee fighter (at least for now). The swordsman will be relatively cheap to get (and can be bought early on), so he will be useful for early defence and exploration.

Additionally we will also be introducing a pistoleer unit. A little more expensive than the swordsman, the pistoleer will have his namesake pistol to fight with, which will have a lower range and damage than the musket, but which will reload faster, and the pistoleer will also get faster movement speed than the musketman. 

With these three units, we wanted to make sure that they weren’t simply set up as countering each other in a rock-paper-scissors manner, but rather that each one of them could win against the others as long as they were utilised correctly. Once up close (e.g. by walking them around a hill and avoiding line of sight) the swordsman’s melee damage should outstrip the other units close up. Likewise, the pistoleer should excel in mid-range combat, making him a perfect choice when fighting among buildings or large trees. Finally, the musketman should be the best choice to fight in open areas, making army composition and tactics in each specific area important. 

Of course, the three new units will also be reflected in the pirates: Initially, it will be swordsmen that will attack you or that will be hidden in the jungle close to your base - but as you are increasing your wealth or advancing further into the island, you will face more and more pistoleers and musketmen as you go.

We may be adjusting all of this for balance as we do more testing, of course, but as always, let us know what you think!

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 40 - Skinning and Rigging
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/eede52cd9cd94f504ac3830bbbd579b41d05b042.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
It is John again, and time for another delve into the art side of the game. 

As you may have noticed from our updates and posts, our focus for the art has shifted between various things (e.g., particle effects, mountain rocks, etc) over the past few weeks and months. This is largely due to the feedback we received from you regarding what it felt like to play the game, as well as us spending our (far too limited) time wherever we felt it was most needed.

With the mountain rocks largely finished, I have now been able to return to one of my bigger, longer term goals: To get the new Villager models in place. I am saying models, instead of singular model, as I have been also working on a female villager to go along with the preview you had of the male villager from a few blogs back. 

As you can see from the screenshot below, a first draft of her has been modelled and partially textured at this point and I have been focusing on skinning the characters and rigging them.

Skinning is when you make an armature (set of bones) and then connect the mesh for the model to those bones so when you move the bone, the mesh moves too. As you can imagine, this does not always work as expected on the first try, and I have been working through many issues with stretching and clipping and trying to get them to work seamlessly. It can be a barrel of laughs, I assure you.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/3898a3a4a315265a8089dd4119d3c4cfca2fe3f3.png[/img]

Rigging is when you take those bones, and set constraints to them, so they move more naturally. Technically, you do not need to rig the bones, and I didn’t for the iteration of the villager in the game currently. I took each bone individually and animated rotation and movement for them to simulate the walking or the shooting that we have. Frankly, I am still impressed with how well they came out considering – and with the rigged armatures, I am hopeful that the new animations will both look more natural, and that we will be able to implement them more smoothly in the game.

In addition to the rigging, I have also set up inverse kinematics, as well as extra bones for more flexible movement. For instance, I have rigged the feet so that the toes initially remain on the ground while the heel tilts, simulating the Villager pushing off with their foot for forward movement. Another good example is the spine curving with different strengths so we better simulate the bend in the back while the hips and shoulders can move independently.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/083ff20395ad50f83038305df954a5c764edde6f.png[/img]

It is a lot more work at this stage - but with the upcoming animation of the characters, it is going to be a great deal easier and quicker to get more natural movements. Additionally, we can plug the inverse kinematics into Unity too - so the characters can react to the different levels of the terrain, so their feet can stick to inclines etc. At the moment, we are not planning to use all of the bones (we are not using the “bones” for the eyes, for example), but as we are continuing development, I hope that we will be able to implement more and more animations to use the full range of options we are giving ourselves with the new system.

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 39 - Specialisations
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/8f5add077e6124961170da0fc2951970c0e7d7fc.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
After alluding to it a few times already, we want to take some time today to elaborate on our plans for coop and specialisations.

While we have been testing the co-op map we are working on, we have noticed how much more engaging it is for us to play together when we need to rely on each other's economies and production in order to progress with the game. 

The map that is currently available to play, Spike Ridge, was created as a versus map, meaning that we made each player location relatively equal and removed from the other player locations. When playing this as a team, it can create some interesting dynamics (where does each player start, and how do we secure the resulting “joint” area from pirates), but for the most part, it feels like you are just playing the game “next to” each other.

Consequently, we have been developing a slightly asymmetric map with a coop vs pirates focus in the past few weeks. There are trees for player one in abundance as well as space to build farms, but little rock and no ore nodes. On player two’s side there are few to no trees to cut for wood and precious little space for farms, but there is an abundance of rock and mining possibilities. We also want there to be more exploration for player two to offset the fact that the side of the map appears more barren. We have hinted at this in previous updates by indicating that there will be pathways through the hills, leading to potential discoveries. ‘Potential’ due to the randomised node placements, so there will be a large chance of something at the end of a path - but what you get (and if anything) is never certain. 

This has, as mentioned before, helped our feeling of playing together, rather than developing separate villages next to one another and remaining mostly independent, and was further aided by us disabling the ability to purchase goods. Waiting on food deliveries to be able to expand more in order to mine Iron to send back to your ally so they can further develop their food production, has made the experience more symbiotic and we have really enjoyed that. 

With that in mind, we have been putting some thought into how we could further this more and we are thinking of using specialisation for each player. For instance, we are thinking of breaking the buildings down into trees of research. The starting branches would need an investment and once unlocked, would enable cheaper construction. So for instance, if it takes 1,000 Coin to unlock the Sawmill, it will make less sense for player two to invest into this building with so few trees on that side of the map. By the time that they expand further into the map and eventually find trees, player one should be so specialised into the Sawmill and it’s associated wood production buildings that it still should make more sense for player two to rely on their ally, rather than now unlocking sawmills for themselves. This should make the games feel more unique per playthrough, depending on what minerals you find, and how you wish to develop your specialisation, while also allowing for a more harmonious development (where it will make sense for one player to grab a newly discovered mineral vein over the other, rather than this becoming a “first come first serve” competition).

Unlocking building specialisations can obviously be further expanded by making efficiency improvements and additional manufacturing processes unlockable as well, but we will go into that in more detail in a future development update.

As always, let us know what you think!

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 38 - Upgrading Mountains
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/daa1dea73698ee2ff299a7afc7855b2934931265.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
As you can see from the screenshot this week, we have been playing with the style we want our mountains to follow. 

We decided early on that sandstone was going to feature prominently for our art style and the fabric of our more grandiose buildings - considering we really enjoyed the references we found of sandstone buildings. Naturally, having sandstone feature heavily in the map would be logical which led us to find the relevant references for sandstone mountains and rock formations. 

There are so many different types of sandstone that this also provides us with some flexibility with different formations on different maps when world building which will be useful for identification and variety. However, our first drive was to combine gorgeous jungle landscapes with the exposed sandstone, which led us to Zhangjiajie National Park (the one that also inspired the environments of Avatar). Consequently, we are thinking of creating formations inspired by the one below. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/2905b23f0cccfe9ae649ef2cfc35ff24c3278992.jpg[/img]

This works for the game jungle style we are aiming for and we have been making the puzzle pieces to start world building with this goal in mind. The triplanar shaders we have worked on help bring together some of the clusters we have been making, and things like the wind and water shaders help bring the worlds to life really quickly. Don’t you love it when a plan comes together?

We are excited about how it is going to look in the end and how it will add charm to the currently featureless mountain ridges we have been working with. 

Now that walking on rocks will also be a major part of movement, we have also reworked the movement, and resolved a known issue of ‘bunny hopping’ up slopes which are too steep for the player, allowing them to climb where we didn’t want them to. This will prove really helpful with defining paths through the mountains and being able to hide secrets for the players to find. Considering how much we have enjoyed exploring the map up until now, we hope this will really build on that. 

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 37 - Map Discoveries
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/d273074f668941eb264b8486ca2fda9ca429f3a5.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
Last week I mentioned that I would give you some more information on how the strategic map interacts with the node system, which I will be doing today.

As it stands, “discovery” in the game is based solely on the player walking across the island by themselves and visually detecting interesting things (chest, ore, pirates). Once found, the player has to remember where they found it, and has to track back to that location if they want to engage with it.

While this will continue to be the case for the very early game, the new strategic map will come in once you place a military HQ. The strategic map will show you the terrain of any explored parts of the island (including the parts you’ve explored before placing the building), giving you information about where to set up defences or be wary of ambushes - where canyons can create a dangerous path or overlooking hills will provide a strategic advantage. Once placed, the military HQ will also allow you to send out scouts to help you with exploration, both to chart areas that are unknown, and to keep track of opponents on an ongoing basis.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/a5827af14fec59f1988f6a186b5c050c6d08df18.png[/img]
(This image shows the current state of a partially revealed map - a little "rough around the edges", but this is how it will work in general)

Resources like trees, rocks that can be broken for stone, fruit trees, etc. are represented as icons on the map to help you get a better understanding of the land and what it has to offer. Resources that spawn randomly will also be shown in this way, e.g. fruit trees, so you will automatically see their locations if you or one of your scouts have gotten close enough (Today's main image shows an area with forest, some fruit trees, and some rocks). 

A more important thing to discover, however, are the ore veins across the island. At the moment, we have rock, iron, gold, and gem veins, and finding one of them can seriously influence decisions about the location of players’ expansions, what type of goods they will produce, or where they choose to defend. Considering their importance, we wanted to not simply have the type of ore vein revealed as your scouts track across the world, but instead, scouts will only reveal that there *is* a type of mineral vein in a location. Once such a location has been marked, the player can visit the location themselves, discovering what type of vein they have found, and make a decision about what to do with it. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/064ae3034ce7b47d72090ad03248f9aee8403843.png[/img]
(This image shows a "spotted" chest between some rocks, as well as an a spot in which an unknown ore type can be found)
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/d5406751081aae163da730873d668778d6a34a7a.png[/img]
(The same image, with the ore vein having been revealed to be a gold vein by the commander)

Finally, there may be spawns of pirates or of chests across the world. Both of those will be revealed by scouts or soldiers, if they have direct line of sight on them (we wouldn't want to give away some of the more hidden chests simply because a scout was within 100 metres of it), or can alternatively be revealed by the commander themselves, if they look directly at it and press a key to spot the chest/pirate.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/665e54a2edb83d444fac88e6efffd95e97443f49.png[/img]
(This image shows 2 pirates having been spotted in a valley with an iron ore vein)

For chests, the location will obviously remain the same until the materials from the chest are collected. However, pirates or enemy soldiers will move around the map freely, which means that the icon on the map will only ever track the last location in which a pirate/soldier has been spotted. As a commander, it will therefore be your responsibility to make sure that the information you have is not too outdated, or to make your plans while keeping in mind that an enemy army may have moved since you last saw it.

Most of this functionality (minus the scouts) is already working in our development build, and I am thoroughly enjoying testing it - especially checking out what nodes have spawned when I see the red crosses for their locations!

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 36 - Randomness
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/93882d797cb72fe5a927c46ad7b01f51a5e0978f.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
As it turns out, I forgot to mention one of the bigger developments in last week’s post, so I will talk about it today: the node manager. 

The node manager is what powers a lot of the randomness in the game. As those of you who have played the game know, there are a number of things that can spawn in random places in the world: iron and gold veins, pirate camps, chests, groupings of banana trees, etc. The randomness of what ends up spawning and where makes each game a little different from the last, and we hope increases replayability. 

Previously, this system wasn't particularly flexible: Each player had a number of positions around them that were considered “player” positions. Each player was guaranteed at least one iron vein, but otherwise, each of the positions had the same probability to spawn iron, a pirate, or a low quality chest. In addition, there were a number of “rich” positions in the middle of Spike Ridge (as well as at the end of our new co-op map), which had equal chances of spawning gold, gems, multiple pirates, high quality chests, etc.

Considering our continuing focus on PvE and a need for some more flexibility, we decided to overhaul this system, and we can now define different probabilities and types of things to spawn for each place in the world. We can also create different “guaranteed” spawns for any arbitrary groups of world positions, and make spawns dependent on each other.

Overall, this means that we can make areas of our worlds a lot more specialised for co-op, and make the rewards of exploration more consistent with the world you are seeing. For example, we can give one player an area with a high chance for mines and rocks, whereas another player gets an area with a high chance for banana groupings or chests containing seeds. Likewise, we will hopefully be able to use this system for Points of Interest in the future, or quest specific spawns e.g. spawning a collection of ruins to explore where appropriate, or spawning a particularly large and useful tree deeper in the jungle. 

With the added work on the strategic map I have been doing over the past week, finding and identifying the random spots across the world has also become a lot more interesting, but I will explain that in more detail next time.

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 35 - The Strategic Map
notes.content:

[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
After telling you a lot about our plans over the past few weeks, today will be focused on what we’ve actually accomplished in that time.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/5ad7f11e8906dd98a92f7df1402a827504c971a9.png[/img]
(Closer-up of the map. You can see rock deposits, trees/forests, and fruit tree groupings around the starting area)
