notes.title: Weekly Update 34 - Ammo
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/6d8d91d9380051c676167cd2bbf58620a75678c9.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
After promising it for the past 2 weeks, I will finally discuss the planned ammo mechanic today. 

Let’s start with our goal: Considering that we were trying to create a “strategy” game, we wanted to make sure that a player got an advantage not by bringing more units or firing first, but we wanted to encourage players to utilise as many strategic advantages as they could (flanking, high ground, assessment of what your opponent is doing) in order to give them an edge in battle.  One of the more important considerations in this regard in a “real” war is logistics. Being able to keep your troops supplied and fed during an expedition or conquest is vitally important at a very top down level, so creating and securing your supply lines is not to be taken lightly. This is also something that can be decided on outside of the chaos of combat itself, which moves it to being a strategic choice rather than a reaction. As a result, it was important to us to have an aspect of “supply” in the game. 

Initially, we wanted to cover this with Coin being brought to Barracks. We moved away from this before even publishing the game, as we made Coin virtual rather than a physical good. What we replaced it with was food, which needed to be provided to the market to supply Towers and Barracks. However, with Barracks, there is no need to further supply your soldiers as you walk them halfway across the island, as long as the Barracks in the base receive a steady supply of food. The way we have countered this is to make soldiers less effective the further they get from their Barracks, in the hopes that this would lead players to create forward operating bases and build their Barracks there. Unfortunately, this system is very unintuitive, and difficult to visualise for players. It is unclear how effective a soldier is at any point, whether they will perform worse if moved across this hill, or whether moving a Barracks is actually worth it.

So, we decided to replace the efficiency mechanic with an ammo mechanic. Every soldier will now have a certain amount of ammo in their inventory, which they will use with each shot. Once they run out of ammo, they will default to melee attacks, which will be less powerful (and more dangerous) than shooting from a range. In order to resupply with ammo, they will need to get close to a Barracks or a supply building, at which point their inventory gets refilled from the building’s inventory. This will mean that ammo either needs to be supplied to a forward base in order to minimise the time the soldiers take to get to ammo, or the army will need to be moved back across the entire island in order to regain its efficiency. 

This also opens up new dynamics regarding producing ammo to start with, but we can also supplement this with research into better ammo, the need for access to better materials (nitre, sulfur, etc) for better ammo, and supplying your armies halfway across the island with the chance to have the shipment intercepted will hopefully make for some more strategic and considered gameplay (especially when you have a map and scouts to tell you about this). Beyond this, the commander will of course also require ammo as discussed before, which should stop the FPS legends among you from dominating too early (until you’ve set up the supply lines to support it!).

We will talk more about what we have gotten done over the past 2 weeks in the next post, but the current image is a little sneak peak of the latest version of the stone mason.

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 33 - Embracing PvE
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/043950f287dc923494750c51a33638b7d230d9dd.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
When we originally started writing these weekly updates on our development, we were pretty worried that we may not have enough to say each week. As it turns out, in recent weeks we’ve had the exact opposite problem - with everything that’s been going on, we have had a really hard time actually getting into everything. 

So, instead of getting into our idea for ammo changes (next week, I promise), let me actually take a step back and communicate what is probably the most important change we have decided on since launching the game: Embracing Player versus Element (PvE) gameplay.

When we first started development, we wanted the game to be match based. We assumed that most people would want to play with/against their friends, and that they would want to play in matches lasting about an hour or two. After running our open beta, we very quickly realised that this was not the case. Most of our testers much preferred to play single player games, and the most requested feature was coop, rather than anything furthering Player versus Player (PvP) gameplay. Consequently, we added save games to the game before launch, as well as Pirate attack waves, to give at least some singleplayer features to those who were requesting them.

After launching the game last year, we realised that the same was true for most people who had bought the game. While some players were very interested in the PvP side, the majority of players played singleplayer, and we tried to fix and add features for the singleplayer side as much as we could. Since then, we have introduced team play, and we have created a new map (not yet available to players) which is a lot more coop/PvE focused. 

As stated above, we want to embrace this further. Focusing on PvE (and coop, cause we like playing together ourselves) will allow us to balance the game a lot more toward longer games (20ish hours), and to focus on creating a challenge that is a little less “balanced” for every player. This does not mean that we will entirely abandon PvP matches, but we will prioritise balancing and designing the game with PvE in mind, and maybe create a separately balanced PvP mode further down the line.

One of the most important changes we have made in this direction already is to remove the ability to purchase goods from the port. Having the ability to buy materials was a way for us to balance competitive matches so a player would be able to focus on one part of the game/economy without boxing themselves in - however, with PvE focused gameplay, having to get every bit of material you need yourself creates a much more interesting challenge, and allows coop players to specialise more, and help each other out by sending needed goods back and forth (The image today is an example of me specialising in food/farming for a game with John, who focused on mining and stone).

With this out of the way, I think that the updates of the next weeks will be a lot easier to understand in context, and I am looking forward to hearing what you think. 

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 32 - Upgrading the Commander
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/c6a5566e119c49af31ec57c79729e03ec1fd85b2.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
Over the past few weeks, John and I have been discussing the larger structure of the game. After we had to scramble to include most of the mechanics we wanted to for the game’s launch, the RTS update (v0.8) will bring in the last major new mechanics (the maps and scouting), and we have finally started to think about balance and tidying up the existing mechanics.

As part of this ongoing endeavour, we have decided to change some of the ways in which the commander works. As I mentioned last week, the commander will now require food every minute, to bring him in line with the villagers and add a little more of a survival challenge to the exploration game. Last week, we also decided to make the commander’s pistol more accurate, increased the rate at which the commander can gather stone, and we are planning to generally improve the commander’s abilities over the coming weeks.

For some context: We had originally decided that we did not want the commander to be too powerful - we wanted to encourage a game in which the focus was on commanding your people, not on running around like Rambo and dealing with problems by yourself. Especially with combat, we knew that we would have to work around seasoned FPS players potentially defeating entire armies by themselves, and we wanted to make sure that the RTS part of the game would have a larger impact on the success of a player. 

After some thought, our approach to preventing an FPS god from dominating the battlefield and sniping with their pistol, was to introduce an inaccuracy with the flintlock weapons. If fast and accurate firing from afar would not necessarily be successful, we hoped that players would focus more on using their soldiers. While we noticed that this was rather frustrating on a few occasions, we thought that this was the lesser evil in order to prevent people from spawn camping their enemies etc. 

Over the past few weeks, however, we have been discussing embracing the commander’s role a little more. Just because the commander may be able to do something better than an individual villager (I certainly feel good about being better than an NPC), the sheer quantity of villagers can easily outstrip a commander’s individual contribution and still maintain a “command” focused game. We have also been introducing a range of changes which naturally help to mitigate the player’s FPS advantages in combat. One of these changes was the introduction of health pools and varying damage on guns. With this, we can balance the impact that a player’s gun has per shot (the pistol currently does 60 damage instead of insta-killing), which makes the commander less of a threat to start with.

We have also been discussing introducing ammo to the game, both to provide progression (upgrades) and bonuses to find in the jungle (improved ammo in a chest would be a nice perk until it runs out) This also has an advantage of reinforcing the supply chains we have been wanting to encourage. A lot of factors have gone into this, but we will be discussing them a little more next week. Considering the commander will now need ammo as well (or will do when we implement it!) this means it is less of a risk that they will be running over to the enemy commander at the start and be a nuisance. 

As a result of these changes, we now made the pistol accurate. John has been the first to agree that it is a lot more pleasant now. Being able to actually trust your gun to hit where you aim is a big change, and we are thinking of adding some damage changes to the gun to make it even better (e.g. higher damage when closer to the opponent - that way sneaking up on a pirate will actually have a benefit).

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 31 - Hunger
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/3216cb60cefc3d35c73a58d3fe89205cff60978e.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
This week, we want to share with you some further depth into our thoughts regarding food.

As you will remember from last week, my testing made me realise that the food dynamic at the moment was rather badly balanced. With just 4 fields, I was able to sustain a population of 70 villagers, and that seemed like too many villagers for so few fields. We had been thinking about making the food mechanic more interesting for a while, so with last week’s decision to also change balancing, we’ve decided to make some changes:

The first change we want to make is to make food a requirement for the commander. With the introduction of health in one of the recent updates, the commander can consume food from his inventory in order to regain health, but we had decided not to make the food a “survival” requirement at the time. We want to change this now, so the commander uses a unit of food each minute, just like the villagers, which will either recover health if it is available, or “damage” health if it is not. 

Further, we want to rebalance the existing food production toward being a little more involved while providing a little less for each step. As a result, we will reduce the amount of food produced per field, but with fields being cheaper. We will likely add some variation to the fields, so choosing to plant tomatoes over potatoes will lead to a quicker harvest but with a smaller payoff (both yielding basic vegetables), etc. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/cc1908cfa805e9f6464f8fca775d609e3e4e5af8.png[/img]
(The new mechanic will add the commander to the regular food consumers, and will introduce the optional kitchen for food refinement)

Adding to this change, we also want to introduce an additional mechanic with “cooking”. In particular, this will allow players to combine the “base” food of fruit, vegetables, meat, and grains in various recipes to create meals. We will need to balance this once we’ve implemented it, but we are thinking that these meals could last longer, and/or provide more health recovery, and/or provide distinct advantages (e.g. faster construction speed when eaten). This will also provide further ‘flavour’ for exploration with the possibility of finding recipes and new foods to better advance through the game.

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 30 - Balancing Food
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/8b8ce6716fb97c61d930d72386e686de02d9a119.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
Our work last week was largely focused on continuing towards the map/RTS update, some testing, and sounds.

After I mentioned last week that we were planning to decrease the cost and efficiency of the wooden tier, I decided to test that idea during the week (A screenshot from my game above). I decreased the cost of the wood tier buildings and the bags of seed for vegetables and wheat, decreased the yield of most buildings, and played to see how it felt. Overall, I think this was already a big improvement. Having to build more buildings early on meant that the early game wasn’t as slow as usual, and I had to make a lot more frequent, smaller decisions about what I wanted to do. I also needed to continuously balance whether to invest in more production, more food, or more defence, which was exactly what the early game should be.

However, this balancing test also showed me that the food needed to be balanced further. At the moment, a single vegetable field can sustain up to 10 villagers, while a single wheat field (with mill and bakery) can sustain 40. That means that my meagre 4 fields (3 vegetable and 1 wheat) were able to sustain 70 villagers - which seems like a bit too much. Consequently, we will try to think about how to better balance the food system, which should make it less of a “set and forget” part of the game.

Finally, I should probably also mention that in my 3 hours of playing the game, I did not encounter a single bug! While John likes to say that I treat the game far too gently for it to break, I still think that this is some cause for celebration, considering just how many times I’ve had to fight with bugs over the course of the game’s development (so far).

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 29 - More Shaders and Future Balancing
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/7649dab7aeae5870f49e3e63dc1898a90265c602.png[/img][h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
Last week we made good progress on the tiling system, did some further work on the shader for rivers and waterfalls, and started working on a procedural shader for tree barks (the title image is one of our shader creations). 

We are experimenting with procedural bark for a couple of reasons: Having a shader instead of a texture will mean that we can implement a variety of moss or weather conditions for the trees based on their location; it will mean that we should be able to have different bark on the same asset based on location; and it will remove a resolution limit on larger assets. The latter is most notable currently with the polynesian palm trees. While we love their scale in the game and their presence in the jungle, the bark looks quite pixelated up close. Additionally, when different levels of LOD load in, we are working to make the transitions smoother. 

Considering all of these are still works in progress and rather technical, we want to use this blog to also talk about some higher level considerations of ours. In particular, we want to discuss the depth and balancing of our production chains. At the moment, the amount of buildings we have is the minimum we considered to be viable to make the game work when we planned it out at the start of the project. Production chains are rather limited, and most of the early buildings are rather expensive while also giving you a really high rate of return. 

When John and I have been playing the game as a team, we tried to specialise on certain aspects (exploration vs base building), which has made us realise how few decisions the base builder has to make in the early game before their economy starts to bring in money. Considering the starting capital of 2k and the cost of e.g. a farm and seeds, it generally isn’t possible to place more than one field before you run out of money - which is obviously not a great way to start the game.

With that in mind, we are planning to adjust the balancing of the early game (wooden tier) to being much cheaper while also having less of a payoff. This should also mean that you need more space and more villagers to produce goods compared to the latter tier production facilities, which will give a nice incentive to upgrade and will mean that villages will have to grow quickly from the very beginning.

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 28 - Fog of War on Maps
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/20554855065e91b03fc6b52d59037c3a8d1a77c6.png[/img][h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
With Easter holidays and lots of backend work, there unfortunately isn’t much to show this week - but we have been working on some considerations for the new mapping system which I will go into.

The new map system is going to require us to implement a system similar to what you will know from many RTS games as the difference between an unrevealed/revealed map, as well as fog of war. However, since you will be missing the ability to look at your units in real time in our game, we will need to adjust this system to operate more on a scale: Information about enemy soldiers will come in with an initial delay, after which they become increasingly outdated unless another scout brings in more information. 

Ultimately, we have decided to create a tile based system for this: We will divide the map into grids (on the backend, you won’t be able to see this in game), which means we can keep track of when your scouts were last able to see a given part of this grid. Let’s say, for example, that your scout last had eyes on grid “B” about 5 minutes ago, and that he was able to see 1 pirate in this grid. Since 5 minutes in the game are not a lot of time, the pirate’s icon on the map will probably be shown in a strong colour. Once  another 10 minutes pass, the information will be more outdated, and the icon will fade. Once another scout gets eyes on the same grid “B”, the map will either show the icon in a strong colour again, or update to show that the pirate is no longer there.

Likewise, the map will update if the scout ends up finding the same pirate in grid “C” a little later - for this, we decided that pirates and enemy soldiers should be recognised uniquely, i.e. you won’t have 5 icons on your map which represent the same pirate who was seen in 5 different places. Instead, your scouts will automatically know that the pirate was the same they had seen before, and the icon will move accordingly.

We’d love to hear your thoughts on the map concepts and will explain a little more next time!

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 27 - Maps
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/c0fe040a5d7dddf984898d6f613488bf1098644f.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
As you can see from today’s image, last week was all about creating the new maps for the RTS update. 

We maintain that we are going to avoid having an RTS style minimap (showing the whole map at a glance and allowing you to react instantly), as we want the game to remain focused on interpreting and anticipating - but in order to interpret and strategise, we need a way for the player to get information about the world and to be able to tell their soldiers what to do. Working from the real world in which the creation of maps by scouts and the ability of a commander to tell their soldiers to take position based on a map are pretty straightfoward, we have therefore decided to include two “maps” of the world:

The first map will be accessible from the commander’s book, and will show the area immediately around the commander’s position. This map will make it easier to give instructions to your armies when they are closeby (showing what you can see and allowing you to fine tune manoeuvres in the area), or to find that mine you previously marked that you could swear was around here somewhere (this is not a problem we are specifically trying to fix for John. At all.) However, the map will not show you much more than you would be able to see when you are looking around you.

The current state of this map can be seen above - we worked to show the height of the terrain, as well as the extent of the water, and you can start to see some of the trees drawn in as brown dots. We will continue adding other icons over the next week, create a system through which you can order your soldiers in this view.

The icons for the maps are going to be hand drawn to keep in the style of the hand drawn buildings in the commanders book, so there is a sense that you or the scouts have drawn the map as they are progressing around the island. We will draw out varieties of the icons and place them in the game to see how they are feeling and iterate on them as needed. We look forward to hearing feedback from our players too, so we know which ones are working or falling short and can adjust as necessary. 

The second map will be a larger scale map of the whole island as you may be used to from RTS games. However, unlike in traditional games, this won’t be a part of your UI (or as easily accessible as the commander’s book). Instead, you will have to review the map at the Military HQ, and it will include all the information the Scouts have currently accumulated (variable information will timeout). Imagine this as a large map on a physical table as you may have seen it in films about wars in times of muskets and cannons, which has cute little wooden copies of your armies on it that you can move around with a big stick.

We will update you on the progress of the maps again next week (and maybe even the one after), but we hope this will be an interesting topic for most!

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 26 - Building Attacks
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/6cd016f51d70ad0c71455e63850d7ad620695611.png[/img][h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
Last week has been largely focused on continuing work on building attacks and bug fixes, but I am also going to talk a little bit about the current state of our animations.

Starting with the bug fixes, we found a decent number of bugs in the latest version, which were luckily pretty easy to fix (e.g. pirates not attacking on Spike Ridge, water not drowning the player on Spike Ridge, etc). As a result, we will be uploading another update tomorrow evening (after some more testing), which will include the aforementioned fixes as well as the new pirate mechanics.

Secondly, work on the building attacks has progressed nicely. At the moment, pirates will attack buildings if they get close to them and there are no soldiers or villagers nearby. If soldiers or villagers are nearby, they will prioritise shooting them first, then turn to the buildings.

Building attacks are now based on the soldier/pirate getting close to the building (closer than they would come to shoot), and then each attack removes some health from the building. The range and damage will obviously be adjustable for additional units in the future, but the general setup will likely remain the same. 

One pretty apparent gap at the moment is our lack of animations for this. When finished, we want the pirates to throw a torch at the building for the attack animation, and for buildings to get gradually damaged to show their hitpoints. However, animations take quite a bit of time to make, and considering how close we are to implementing the new villager model, we want to focus on making the animations for the new model, rather than having to make the animations twice. 

Under normal circumstances, we would simply hold off on releasing the new mechanic until we have the animation ready. However, I consider the building attack to be a very important part of my upgrade of the pirates. Therefore, adding it, even without an animation, gives players a chance to experience pirate attacks as they are intended. Let us know your thoughts on this, however - we are always happy to receive feedback on our approach.

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 25 - Building Hitpoints
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/c088049c6704d4b7f89a948736da846111ba6485.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
With last week’s update wrapping up a lot of the smaller improvements that we wanted to make ahead of the bigger update, this week was largely focused on attacks against buildings.

First of all, thank you to everyone who gave us feedback on last week’s update, it seems that the new look of the ocean was particularly attractive to many! With that in mind, I have already worked on a shader for our foliage, which will include wind movement - and John has also started looking into a way to decrease the harsh shadow changes in the tree canopies.

Regarding the attacks against buildings, those of you who have played the game against other players (not too many competitive players around though!) know that soldiers currently attack buildings by only standing in front of the door. If they haven’t been killed by an opponent after 30 seconds, the building gets destroyed. 

This approach was largely a result of us thinking about how to simplify the way a building would get destroyed by marauders in the real world (most likely by setting fire to it with a torch), which we wanted to emulate by them having to survive in close proximity to the building for a little while. The desire for a “realistic” approach was somewhat driven by the first person perspective of the game, and trying to avoid anything that would break immersion too badly (and who doesn’t get immersed in 30 seconds of animation-less waiting?).

With the RTS update on the horizon and a desire to improve the behaviour of pirates, we have now decided to go more in the direction of a traditional RTS: In the past week, I added hitpoints to buildings, which can be removed by attacks by multiple enemy units, and villagers will repair damaged buildings (see image above). As a result, it will be possible to have more than one soldier (or pirate) attacking a building, and more attackers will destroy the building quicker.

In the coming week(s), we will be working on implementing this as a default behaviour for pirates as they come across your settlements.

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 24 - Water
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/8a6b1372f9ec65ee5e5b14af5cfa8db83d3fa044.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
While this past week has been rather hectic in our non-game-developer lives, we have managed to get the game ready for the latest patch, which was quite a bit of work, as we had introduced many new features on our test map, which hadn’t been implemented on Spike Ridge or the Tutorial map yet.

Among the many changes that are going to be uploaded tonight are the new Stonemason (functionality is finished, but the model is a placeholder that will be improved upon); the new health mechanic (you can find your “health bar” in the character section of your book, eat food by clicking on it from your player inventory); the new water shader we talked about (also not final, but better than before, as seen in the picture); team play (including sending resources to your allies); the performance improvements we promised; and many, many bug fixes.

With all of this done, we are going to be redoubling our efforts to work on our first big update (the RTS update, 0.8!). Since many of these features have only been tested internally so far, we are expecting that some of you will be finding bugs, please let us know and we will fix them as they come up. 

We are looking forward to hearing what you think of the patch!

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 23 - Improved Gun Visuals
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/19647a13ec1a1e6e35efdd8c21107999c1f07060.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
Last week was largely focused on further bug fixes in the new systems leading up to our patch the next week. However, there is another update to visuals as a result of our work with the particle system we would like to show off today: Gun smoke and impacts.

Those of you who have played the game (or even watched the trailer), know that our guns so far were just firing a white line from the shooter to the target. Until the most recent update when I moved the start of the line to the barrel of the gun, the line was even drawn from the soldiers’ chest to the target. 

All of this is now updated with smoke and a muzzle flash coming from the soldiers’ guns, and an impact effect at the place the gun has hit. The impact effect will also change between what has been hit (a blood effect for hitting units, and a puff of smoke for other materials). This update is particularly important with the new health system, as shooting someone doesn’t necessarily kill them anymore, and having the little impact effect as indication of whether the shot has hit is important.

The effects are not yet finalised, but we think the looks are a massive improvement from what we had before, so we will leave it in roughly this state for now.

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 22 - Stone Cutting
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/d4ca114b50cb174ac63ceedc3fa7614cf3af3976.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
Last week has been largely dedicated to finally implementing the Stone Mason, as well as testing the new team play part of the game.

Firstly, implementing the Stone Mason and villagers collecting Stone from boulders has opened up a big additional feature for maps: The possibility for us to close off certain valleys and walkways with rocks, which can be cleared by the players over the course of the game. This will allow us to more effectively separate players in the early game, delay access to certain areas, and help players funnel their opponents in more creative ways.

Secondly, as we mentioned in last week’s update, we have been trying to test the new teamplay. While this has led to a ton of straightforward fixes and improvements (having changed added a lot of functions led to many new issues), we also wanted to test what it feels like to play the game together, for balancing and gameplay concerns. 

One of the outcomes of this, for example, was a new chest that has been placed next to the Port. Unlike normal chests, this one does not disappear when everything is taken out, and players on the same team can use it to quickly exchange goods with each other when needed. 

Another outcome was a change to the movement of players: With one player being more focused on exploration on the new map, we realised that it can feel quite rewarding to find your way up onto a mountain to scout the terrain ahead of you - but with players being able to just stand on the side of a cliff, the feeling of risk and accomplishment was somewhat reduced. As a result, we have implemented a new sliding mechanic, which makes scaling mountains more difficult and more dangerous - but will hopefully lead to better immersion and more enjoyable scouting!

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 21 - Particles and Shaders
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/9a6285a58d0b0202067c7c900f714aa37883d5ab.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
After last week’s unexpected improvements to performance, we have finally been able to dedicate some time this week to creating graphics improvements. 

First of all, we were able to start implementing a number of particle effects - as showcased in this blog’s screenshot - which are helping to bring some life into the maps. Where at the moment, we still have primarily static art; falling leaves, fire, smoke, and a range of other particle effects should help us bring the world a little more to life before we even get to better animations (after the new villagers), so this is an intermediate step we have really enjoyed putting into the game. They make a big atmospheric improvement already and we are excited to see them combined with wind moving through the foliage and vegetation.

Secondly, we decided to also focus on shaders a little more than we had so far. We are not finished yet and will probably showcase it with the blog next week - but for our first improvement, we now have rolling waves and crests of foam with the water lapping against the shore. It is already looking a lot better and we look forward to seeing where we can get to before shipping it.

We have also been pushing hard to get the new teamplay focused asymmetric map up to speed and this means that we can test how the new gameplay mechanics work with an ally. Our goal for the PvE team game is to give different starting conditions to each player, making you rely on each other, and we are currently testing and trying to enhance that experience. We have already found some bugs with the way that teamplay works and we are working on cleaning them up and creating a balanced experience before we upload the next patch. 

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 20 - Artefact Mode
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/f5ee00073a660bbd4128d1b58e3bb12e9fca8738.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
Last week has been a little busy in our day jobs, but we managed to do quite a bit on the game nonetheless:

First of all, I managed to create a team victory condition, so people playing together will now share benefits, such as the unlock of their seed market, as well as winning the game. Considering this required quite a few adjustments of the underlying system, I also got around to creating a new victory condition: Artefact mode. In artefact mode, we will have a single, heavily defended chest on the map, and whoever manages to get to it first, wins. This should change competitive gameplay to something more militaristic, but it should also allow coop play (and singleplayer) to have a more specific goal than simply making money (without the time constraint that comes with a human opponent). 

Secondly, we also managed to do a decent amount of testing of the latest changes to soldiers and pirates, and have addressed a few of the more specific bugs as they came up. We are pretty confident that the new system will work very robustly by the time we patch the game.

Finally, I had to address a multiplayer bug that randomly started happening on the test branch, which prevented players from starting the game at certain times. John has also been continuing his work on the performance improvements for the plants, so while we aren't fully happy with the current states of the plants, we are seeing much smoother gameplay across most systems. This will carry across when we improve the trees and plants so they are built off the same performance principles. 

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 19 - Rudimentary Team Play
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/52e3029aedf885d758b5f4be975321b87964a063.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
Last week, I joked that there had been a dip in quality from John’s hijack of the weekly update - judging from the approval our respective posts received, I may have to concede that art is more appealing than function, and John may get to do another update in the future ;).

Without further ado, let’s get into the changes we made this week:

[h3]Unexpected team play[/h3]
While team play was originally lower on our list of priorities, I decided to take a quick look into making teamplay work, and I got surprisingly far. At this point, players can choose their teams at the start of the game, and soldiers within the same team won’t shoot each other. Further, players within the same team can set up movement of goods between their warehouses, allowing them to support each other with resources when needed. Once I add a joint victory condition to the mix, we will be able to upload this for some basic 2v2 gameplay, as well as a new coop map we are working on. Stay tuned.

[h3]Further soldier updates[/h3]
Since the patch, we have already worked on improving the soldiers further: With our overall goal of strategic combat in mind, we wanted to A) make it possible to gain a combat advantage through assessing the environment correctly in the moment, and B) make it possible to gain a combat advantage through setting your long term logistics up in the right way.

To achieve point A, we have already added a damage bonus for units on high ground (this meant that we had to implement health bars as well), so placing units along the hill of a choke point will actually give a big advantage to their effectiveness. The inclusion of health bars means that units (and the player) won’t necessarily die from a single shot, and that food also takes the role of healing units/the player. Units continue to eat 1 food per minute and heal/take damage depending on whether the food is available. Players can heal by using food that is in their inventory.

To achieve point B, we made soldier accuracy scale with the distance from their barracks. If your barracks are well placed, and your soldiers fight close to them, their accuracy will be highest, and they should have a distinct advantage over their opponents. Order your soldiers to track half-way across the map and be miles away from their barracks, and their accuracy will suffer. As a result, you will have to create forward bases for successful (and effective) attacks, which will require you to provide food and protection to these outposts as well.

[h3]Unexpected performance update[/h3]
Finally, John unexpectedly got around to making some improvements to the foliage this week, which ended up drastically improving performance. From what we can tell from our limited tests so far, we are looking at approximately 40% higher frame rates, which should really help some of the people with slower computers. Of course we will continue to work on performance throughout, but this was an unscheduled improvement we are very pleased with.

We will keep you updated on the developments, and as always, are looking forward to your feedback about the game and our plans!

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 18 - Soldier and Pirate Improvements
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/7ca1bde857092104442fe824b98aa5538ed4eb3b.png[/img]
[h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
After last week’s unfortunate dip in update quality, I am happy to report that John is busy working on the villager bodies, and I am back in charge of writing the update.

As briefly mentioned by John, last week saw the release of a patch just ahead of the blog, and a second smaller patch to fix some MacOS issues the day after. The patch included the Quest System (which you can check in the new Tutorial), the Localisation System (which you can’t see yet), and the first parts of the new soldier/pirate behaviour. Considering we wrote about the first two before, I’ll focus on the soldier behaviour today. In the process of writing this, I got a little carried away, so consider this part 1 of 2!

[h3]Soldier behaviour before:[/h3]
Those of you who have played the game know that the behaviour of the soldiers and pirates used to be a bit of a weak point of the game: Pirates across the island were stationary, and would shoot you when you got into view (mind you that they had eyes in the backs of their head and would “look” through shrubbery). Pirates in attack waves and your soldiers were a little better, insofar as they at least had a target to move towards when they weren’t shooting.

[h3]Soldier behaviour now:[/h3]
At this point, we have entirely revamped the soldier/pirate behaviour. Most importantly, soldiers/pirates now have a field of view toward their front. If you approach them from behind, they won’t be able to see you, unless you make a lot of noise. Noise is dependent on how you move (crouching makes the least noise, running makes the most noise), what you move through (avoiding shrubbery is your best bet to not make noise), and how you act (shooting or cutting down trees makes noise). 

If one of the soldiers/pirates hears a noise, they will go to investigate. Depending on how close and how loud the noise was, they may lose interest sooner or later - but if they see you, they will start shooting. If you manage to escape, they will pursue you up to the last location where they saw you. Visibility is blocked by trees and (partially, to different extents) by shrubbery, so if you are crouching or not moving at all, foliage becomes your friend. Once the pirates have not seen or heard you for a while, they will return to their original location. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/c757478799566ae1bef73887033d01a4fd092b46.jpg[/img]
(As you can see in this sketch, trees will block vision, shrubbery will partially block vision, with multiple bushes giving you full cover, and noises will be investigated only if they are loud enough)

Overall, this has already made the world a lot more organic and interesting. Fighting in the middle of the jungle can become a lot more dangerous, as pirates from a wide area can hear you exchange gunshots with a solitary pirate and come to his aid. If you find a solitary pirate close to your base or soldiers, you can now bait them into walking right into an ambush - simply get their attention and stay ahead of them.

We will dedicate the next weekly update to telling you more about the soldier behaviour, so you have something to look forward to ;).

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 17 - Toward a New Villager
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/98d097e1129716f5ecb9cef6e2db5b2129982a27.jpg[/img][h1]Hey everyone![/h1]
I (John) am hijacking the blog this week, You can hear more about the marvellous adventures of Phil next week. We have a lot to cover. 

As you can see by this week's blog cover photo, We have an update for the character model. I have put a few of the developments next to one another for comparison below, showing how they have evolved as we have gone along. 

When Phil dragged me into this project, telling me I was going to be responsible for the artwork, we really didn’t know what that entailed. As I had no idea how blender worked and was making our initial building prototypes in Sketchup, we set the bar as low as we thought would still work for immersion - and intended to make an internally consistent art style which I was going to be able to achieve. 

Problem was, I really started to enjoy Blender and the more I learnt about the software, the more I wanted to push myself. So even though we started with a low poly art style in mind, and created the first bunch of assets that way - we soon realised I was going to be able to do more. This brings about a couple of issues such as needing to upscale all of the existing artwork (which has been happening steadily with still a long way to go) and trying to determine where we were going to draw the line in the sand. If we have some art work modelled to a high standard, it will contrast against lower standard pieces and the inconsistency can result in a muddled art style. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/e6f1487b5f8183bb15252b79807bdd895964511a.jpg[/img]

We decided one approach to defining this limitation for our artwork, was to model what I thought to be the hardest element first, to a limit we were comfortable with - then bring everything else up to that level. Which is why we focused on the character first as people can be problematic. Hence the nightmare fuel in the progression photos - I have needed to upskill and learn proportion and better representation of human form (though I think the nightmare fuel one would make a good mutant villain ;) ). We have settled on the design we like and I am going to work on retopologizing the high poly sculpt (As seen in the topmost image), and then texturing it, putting it onto a new rig and animating it. Then we will drop it in the game and replace the villagers. 

Once that is done - we can work on a pirate model and then start iterating through different models for the pirates and variety for the villagers. Let us know what you think! Among that series of improvements, I shall also be bringing the other art up to this level.

We wanted a strong looking, wise but kind character to begin with and have focused on a strong nose and brow with kindly, aged eyes. We will iterate hairstyles (and hats for professions) to add variety to this villager before I can add further models. 

We have also just uploaded the latest patch which includes the long awaited soldier improvements. They will now pursue you if they hear you (running is louder than crouching), and they need to actually see you in order to shoot at you. As a result of them investigating sound, the middle has also become a lot more deadly as we have found out in testing ;).

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 16 - Possibilities of the Quest System
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/884fecebf5b36434c2c10361346e6e2008a05dce.png[/img]
[h1]Hi everyone![/h1]
Last week has been very productive once again, and we are looking forward to continuing on this trajectory this week.

We managed to rebuild the existing Tutorial under the new quest system. However, the new quest system meant that we were able to include a lot more detail and feedback into the tasks and explanations. Rather than having a few tasks and a bunch of long walls of explanations, we were able to break a lot of it down and guide potential users more than before. 

The new options also meant that we could go into more detail to explain the game, for example showing worker management and the worker overview, which we barely mentioned in the previous version. As a result of being more granular and having additional explanations, the Tutorial went from 20 steps to about 120 under the new system - and we are very excited to see what people think. If you happen to have enjoyed the Tutorial before (or really didn’t like it), consider playing it again after the next patch to let us know what you think! ;)

Another thing that excited us about working on the Tutorial this week was finally seeing the possibilities of the new quest system in action. Quests will consist of multiple steps, and each step can be individually displayed and tracked, can enable or disable objects in the game, buildings that can be constructed, and give rewards for completion or punishment for failure - hopefully allowing us to complete some compelling and intuitive narratives within the game world. For the Tutorial, this meant that we could highlight UI elements we wanted to draw attention to, enable arrows in the world when we wanted to point players to a specific building or area, and enable chests and pirates at specific times.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/f79568280e1ab83b3a2c9e91380dccd5920a1555.png[/img]
(An example of the highlights in the book to better show parts of the Tutorial)

While we are (loosely) planning on including quests in the regular game as of the second major update from now (after the soldier and maps update), creating quests should also give us a good idea for how we want to structure specific tasks within the campaign we are planning for in the long run. We look forward to updating you with more next week!

Until next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update 15 - Happy New Year!
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38555898/e920ffb37fe3ce0f4e405c71c539e9659822cb98.png[/img]
[h1]Hi everyone![/h1]
First off: Happy new year! I hope that everyone’s year will be the best one yet.

Despite a few disruptions last week, John and I have been able to make some good progress. John worked on the new map as promised, and he also updated the medium house to have a little more detail and look less flat. 

In addition to the ongoing work on the Tutorial, I have also been able to refactor and update the code of the processing buildings (Mill, Bakery, Smelter, etc), to make it more robust, but most importantly, to make it more flexible for the future. This will mean that we are going to be able to introduce various new industry buildings fairly easily, which we are planning to do some time after the upcoming RTS update. 

In particular, the new update allows us to move away from single production steps (one input, e.g. flour, into one output, e.g. bread), and will allow us to go into more complex steps (e.g. 5 wood and 1 gold bar into 1 advanced furniture and 2 wood chippings). As you can see from that example, we will also be able to create byproducts to the production steps, which should allow us to create a variety of ways to use new manufacturing buildings, and create more choices for the players.

I am expecting that we will be able to finish the update to the Tutorial this week, so look out for the new patch in the coming days.

Until next week!
